title: 'What Do You Need?' Wednesday: Multitudes, Monet, and Mentos
author: The Beacon, by Episcopal Academy CTL
summary: This is the weekly curated digest from the Center for Teaching and Learning at Episcopal Academy, with an editorial note and a try-this action attached to each item. The first item shows an AI-assisted artwork built from 1,306 faculty sticky notes about what graduates do, rendered as a Monet-style painting of the Chapel in which every brushstroke is a colleague's practice. The second discusses a New York Times essay by Williams College philosopher Joe Cruz asking whether writing is over-weighted as the cultivation of thought, and suggests ninety seconds of peer explanation before collecting an assignment. The third highlights a research paper on emotion regulation and learning from academic failure, with the practical step of letting students jot how a result feels before seeing corrections. The closer uses an xkcd strip about the 10,000 people who hear each common fact for the first time every day, a reminder that repeated routines are not necessarily known by everyone.
points: Faculty-generated data turned into a shared artifact gives colleagues a way to browse and borrow each other's classroom practices.
Writing and speaking can be treated as a sequence rather than rivals, so a short oral explanation before submission can sharpen the written work.
Students who push away negative feelings about a failure also push away what the failure could teach them, so naming the feeling comes before reading corrections.
Each item pairs a reading with a concrete one-minute classroom move, which makes the digest immediately usable.
Early-year routines may feel known by everyone when many students are still hearing them for the first time.
quotes: The result is a Monet-inspired painting of the Chapel at dusk, where every brushstroke is a teacher’s note and the practices colleagues named most often are laid on with a heavier brush.
Stand back to see the Chapel; lean in to read the words of the EA faculty and staff.
Ultimately, his piece reflects some of what we're seeing, particularly in upper school, about writing and talking as a sequence, not rivals.
Before collecting your next assignment, give students ninety seconds to explain its main idea to a peer. Then, let them change one thing based on what they said, or what they heard
In other words, learning from failure is rarely a straightforward process, in part because students who push those feelings away also push away what the failure could teach them.
When you return the next assessment, give students one minute to jot down how the result feels before they look at a single correction.

Nobody is born knowing anything, and nearly every adult eventually learns the things “everyone knows,” so on any given day about 10,000 people in the U.S. are hearing each of those things for the first time.
